items.followUp: Estimate the age of 12 years in seconds.

rubric.why: Award for using the approximate number of seconds in a year.
rubric.description: Converts years to seconds using 365 days per year.
rubric.how: Look for the conversion factors or the approximate seconds-per-year value.

rubric.why: Award for the estimated age in seconds.
rubric.how: Check that the final result is expressed in seconds.

items.followUp: Define force and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Award for identifying momentum as mass multiplied by velocity.
rubric.description: Defines momentum as the product of mass and velocity.
rubric.how: Look for the relation p = mv or an equivalent definition.

rubric.why: Award for the correct SI unit.
rubric.description: States the SI unit of momentum.
rubric.how: Accept kg m/s or its equivalent unit N s.

modelAnswer: Momentum is the product of the mass of a body and its velocity: p = mv.
Its SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).

rubric.why: Award for one valid advantage of friction.
rubric.description: States that friction enables walking or provides grip.
rubric.how: Look for a clear example of friction being useful for movement or grip.

rubric.why: Award for a second valid advantage.
rubric.description: States another advantage, such as writing, braking, or lighting a match.
rubric.how: Accept a distinct valid use of friction.

modelAnswer: Friction between our feet and the ground enables us to walk without slipping.
Friction between a pen or pencil and paper enables us to write.

items.followUp: Explain how to find the resultant of two vectors using the parallelogram rule.

rubric.why: Award for correctly placing the vectors in sequence.
rubric.description: Places the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector.

rubric.why: Award for the correct resultant direction and endpoints.
rubric.description: Draws the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.
rubric.how: Check that the resultant joins the initial tail to the final head.

modelAnswer: Draw the first vector to scale in its given direction.
Place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector, keeping its length and direction unchanged.
The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector.

items.followUp: What is a contact force? Give one example.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing field forces from contact forces.
rubric.description: States that a field force acts without physical contact between interacting bodies.
rubric.how: Look for the absence of physical contact or action at a distance.

rubric.why: Award for a correct example of a field force.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as gravitational, magnetic, or electrostatic force.
rubric.how: Accept any one correct field force.

modelAnswer: A field force acts between bodies without physical contact; it can act at a distance.
Examples include gravitational, magnetic, and electrostatic forces.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the force used in the definition.
rubric.description: Specifies a force of one newton.
rubric.how: Look for 1 N or its words.

rubric.why: Award for the displacement and direction condition.
rubric.description: Specifies a displacement of one metre in the direction of the force.
rubric.how: Look for one metre and displacement along the force.

modelAnswer: The unit of work is the joule (J).
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.

rubric.why: Award for identifying power as work done or energy transferred per unit time.
rubric.description: Defines power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy.
rubric.how: Look for work or energy divided by time.

rubric.why: Award for the correct definition of one watt.
rubric.description: States that one watt equals one joule per second.

modelAnswer: Power is the rate at which work is done.
One watt is the power when 1 joule of work is done in 1 second (1 W = 1 J/s).

items.followUp: A machine receives 500 J of energy and gives 350 J of useful output energy. Calculate its percentage efficiency.

rubric.why: Award for the correct efficiency ratio.
rubric.description: Uses useful output divided by input.
rubric.how: Look for the output-to-input ratio, with useful output specified.

rubric.why: Award for converting the ratio to a percentage.
rubric.how: Check for the percentage factor in the calculation or formula.

modelAnswer: Percentage efficiency = (useful output energy ÷ input energy) × 100%.
For power, percentage efficiency = (useful output power ÷ input power) × 100%.
